newsitem.title: USA: Canada trade minister sees Helms-Burton deferral.
newsitem.headline: Canada trade minister sees Helms-Burton deferral.

text.p: Canada's Trade Minister Art Eggleton said on Wednesday he expected U.S. President Bill Clinton to extend the six-month deferral on enforcing the Helms-Burton law when it ends in January.
Eggleton said he expects Clinton to accede to pleas from Canada and other nations not to enforce the law, which punishes countries that trade with Cuba.

"The president did listen to the protests of Canada, Mexico, the European Union and others when he made the first deferral at the end of August, so I would expect that he would do that again in January," Eggleton told Reuters Television.

Eggleton said in an interview that a lot may depend on the special envoys sent by Clinton around the world to determine what countries are doing to advance the cause of democracy, human rights and open markets in Cuba.
"Deferring means the status quo," Eggleton said.
He also called for the reduction or elimination of U.S. trade remedies like countervailing and anti-dumping tariffs.
"We do have some trade disputes in addition to Helms-Burton," he said. "What we would like is to see some reduction of the use of trade remedies."
He said Canada has been working hard to establish a bilateral trade deal with Chile as a precursor to that country joining the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA).

Canada stepped into the breach to negotiate a bilateral trade deal with Chile along the NAFTA trade deal lines after the lack of U.S. Congressional support took the U.S. away from the bargaining table, Eggleton said.

"So Canada moved in and is working on a bilateral trade agreement with Chile. But we're doing it on the basis of NAFTA...so that when the U.S. is able to come to the table we'll be able to move very quickly to complete that goal set in 1994 of bringing Chile into NAFTA," he said.
